claim: Both D1 and D2 neurons of the anteromedial OT project primarily to the VP and minimally elsewhere.
source: First, using anterograde and retrograde tracing, we show that both D1 and D2 neurons of the anteromedial OT project primarily to the VP and minimally elsewhere.
evidence: Supported by anterograde and retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 1

claim: VP neurons robustly encode reward contingency, but not identity, in low-dimensional space.
source: We find that VP neurons robustly encode reward contingency, but not identity, in low-dimensional space.
evidence: Supported by two-photon calcium imaging data and analysis presented in Figures 3 and 5

claim: OT neurons primarily encode odor identity in high-dimensional space.
source: In contrast, the OT neurons primarily encode odor identity in high-dimensional space.
evidence: Supported by two-photon calcium imaging data and dimensionality analysis in Figures 3 and 5

claim: D1 OT neurons showed larger responses to rewarded odors than other odors.
source: Although D1 OT neurons showed larger responses to rewarded odors than other odors, consistent with prior findings, we interpret this as identity encoding with enhanced contrast.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing differential responses in OTD1 neurons to rewarded odors in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Non-overlapping VP neurons encode reward contingency and licking vigor.
source: Finally, using a novel conditioning paradigm that decouples reward contingency and licking vigor, we show that both features are encoded by non-overlapping VP neurons.
evidence: Supported by data from the lick spout retraction paradigm shown in Figure 6

claim: The OT receives dense DAergic input from the midbrain.
source: In addition to receiving a wide range of inputs from cortical and amygdalar areas (e.g. AI, OFC, BLA, PlCoA, Pir) (Zhang et al., 2017b), it receives dense DAergic input from the midbrain (Ikemoto, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: The OT receives direct input from the mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb.
source: it receives dense DAergic input from the midbrain (Ikemoto, 2007) and direct input from the mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb (Haberly and Price, 1977; Igarashi et al., 2012; Scott, 1981)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Rats self-administer cocaine into the medial OT more vigorously than to any other striatal nuclei.
source: rats self-administer cocaine, a DAergic drug, into the medial OT more vigorously than to any other striatal nuclei (Ikemoto, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Pairing stimulation of midbrain DAergic neurons with an odor drives appetitive behavior towards the paired odor.
source: pairing stimulation of midbrain DAergic neurons with an odor drives appetitive behavior towards the paired odor (Zhang et al., 2017a)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Pairing stimulation of midbrain DAergic neurons with an odor enhances the contrast of the odor-evoked activity.
source: pairing stimulation of midbrain DAergic neurons with an odor drives appetitive behavior towards the paired odor (Zhang et al., 2017a) and enhances the contrast of the odor-evoked activity (Oettl et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: VP receives strong input from the nucleus accumbens.
source: In addition to OT input, VP receives strong input from the nucleus accumbens (Jones and Mogenson, 1980)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: VP receives strong input from the subthalamic nucleus.
source: In addition to OT input, VP receives strong input from the nucleus accumbens (Jones and Mogenson, 1980) and the subthalamic nucleus (Ricardo, 1980; Turner et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: VP receives inputs from several cortical and amygdalar areas that also project to the OT.
source: More recently, it was reported that VP also receives inputs from several cortical and amygdalar areas that also project to the OT (e.g. Pir, BLA, OFC; Stephenson-Jones et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: VP contains GABAergic neurons which respond to positive valence cues.
source: The VP contains GABAergic neurons, which respond to positive valence cues, and glutamatergic neurons, which respond to negative valence cues.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Faget et al., 2018)

claim: VP contains glutamatergic neurons which respond to negative valence cues.
source: The VP contains GABAergic neurons, which respond to positive valence cues, and glutamatergic neurons, which respond to negative valence cues.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Faget et al., 2018)

claim: GABAergic VP neurons drive real time place preference.
source: Consistent with their responsiveness, the GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons drive real time place preference and avoidance, respectively (Faget et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Glutamatergic VP neurons drive real time place avoidance.
source: Consistent with their responsiveness, the GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons drive real time place preference and avoidance, respectively (Faget et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: OT projections were restricted to the lateral portions of the VP.
source: It is also notable that OT projections were restricted to the lateral portions of the VP.
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: OT neurons are more likely to project to the lateral portion of the VP than to the medial.
source: We found predominantly CTB:488, but not CTB::543, labeling in OT soma, indicating OT neurons are more likely to project to the lateral portion of the VP than to the medial.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1E-F

claim: Hardly any neurons within any part of the OT were labeled by CTB injected into the VTA.
source: In contrast, we found that hardly any neurons within any part of the OT were labeled.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data from VTA shown in Figure 1H-I

claim: Both D1 and D2 SPN's of the anteromedial OT project primarily to the lateral portion of the VP and negligibly to other brain areas, including the VTA.
source: Taken together, we conclude that both D1 and D2 SPN's of the anteromedial OT project primarily to the lateral portion of the VP and negligibly to other brain areas, including the VTA.
evidence: Supported by anterograde and retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1

claim: After 3 days of odor-sucrose associations, the animals displayed anticipatory licking behavior primarily during sucrose-paired odors.
source: After 3 days of odor-sucrose associations, the animals displayed anticipatory licking behavior primarily during sucrose-paired odors (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2F and G

claim: By day 6, animals had adapted their anticipatory licking behavior to match the new sucrose-contingency.
source: By day 6, animals had adapted their anticipatory licking behavior to match the new sucrose-contingency (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2G

claim: The accuracy of animals' licks during odor increased across time.
source: Quantification of the animal's licking behavior showed that the accuracy of animals' licks during odor increased across time and was not different across lens-placement groups (Figure 2H, Appendix 1—tables 4 and 5; ANOVA: Fday = 27.64, pday = 2.29e-16, Flens location=2.30, plens location=0.11).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2H

claim: The accuracy of animals' licks during odor was not different across lens-placement groups.
source: Quantification of the animal's licking behavior showed that the accuracy of animals' licks during odor increased across time and was not different across lens-placement groups (Figure 2H, Appendix 1—tables 4 and 5; ANOVA: Fday = 27.64, pday = 2.29e-16, Flens location=2.30, plens location=0.11).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2H

claim: More VP neurons were either excited or inhibited to either sucrose-paired odor than to control or puff-paired odors.
source: We found that more VP neurons were either excited (29.8 ± 4.1%, 36.6 ± 4.0% for SK, ST) or inhibited (24.5 ± 3.0%, 29.4 ± 3.8% for SK, ST) to either sucrose-paired odor than to control or puff-paired odors (7.6–11.1% excited, 8.1–12.9% inhibited; Figure 3D, Figure 2—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: Supported by quantification of neural responses shown in Figure 3D

claim: The percentage of VP neurons that respond to both S odors increases from 6.1 ± 2.2% on day 1 to 34.1 ± 5.1% by the 6th day of imaging.
source: When compared across days, we found that the percentage of VP neurons that respond to both S odors increases from 6.1 ± 2.2% on day 1–34.1 ± 5.1% by the 6th day of imaging (Figure 3E,Appendix 1—table 11).
evidence: Supported by quantification of neural responses across days shown in Figure 3E

claim: The percentage of OT neurons that respond to both S odors in the same direction did not increase through training.
source: By comparison, the percentage of OT neurons that respond to both S odors in the same direction (i.e. excited by both S odors or inhibited by both S odors) did not increase through training.
evidence: Supported by quantification of neural responses across days shown in Figure 3E

claim: OTD1 and OTD2 neurons were more likely to respond to a single odor than they were to respond to both S odors.
source: Furthermore, whereas OTD1 and OTD2 neurons were more likely to respond to a single odor than they were to respond to both S odors (12.6 vs 31.3% in OTD1, 11.8 vs 21.7% in OTD2), VP neurons were more likely to respond to both S odors than to a single odor (34.1 vs 23.3%).
evidence: Supported by quantification of neural responses shown in Figure 3E

claim: VP neurons were more likely to respond to both S odors than to a single odor.
source: Furthermore, whereas OTD1 and OTD2 neurons were more likely to respond to a single odor than they were to respond to both S odors (12.6 vs 31.3% in OTD1, 11.8 vs 21.7% in OTD2), VP neurons were more likely to respond to both S odors than to a single odor (34.1 vs 23.3%).
evidence: Supported by quantification of neural responses shown in Figure 3E

claim: The magnitude of trial-averaged odor responses in the VP were significantly higher for S odors than X or P odors on the last day of imaging.
source: Similarly, we found that the magnitude of trial-averaged odor responses in the VP were significantly higher for S odors than X or P odors on the last day of imaging (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 8, Appendix 1—table 38).
evidence: Supported by quantification of response magnitudes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8

claim: Neither sucrose-pairing nor airpuff-pairing had any impact on the magnitude of odor responses in OTD2 neurons on day 6.
source: By comparison, neither sucrose-pairing nor airpuff-pairing had any impact on the magnitude of odor responses in OTD2 neurons on day 6.
evidence: Supported by quantification of response magnitudes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8

claim: A significant effect of sucrose-pairing on response magnitudes was observed in OTD1 neurons.
source: And though we did observe a significant effect of sucrose-pairing on response magnitudes in OTD1 neurons, both the effect size and significance were weaker than observed in VP.
evidence: Supported by quantification of response magnitudes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8

claim: VP neurons had a high correlation (R2=0.89) between a neuron's responses to SK and ST.
source: VP neurons had a high correlation between a neuron's responses to SK and ST (Figure 3F; R2=0.89).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: For VP neurons, the correlation between responses to SK and ST was much higher than between SK and XK.
source: This similarity was much higher than between the sucrose-paired ketone (SK) and the control ketone (XK) despite the greater structural similarity between SK and XK (Figure 3G; R2=0.33).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3G

claim: For OTD2 neurons, there was a higher correlation between responses to similar molecular structure (SK and XK) than between responses to similar contingency (SK and ST).
source: In contrast, for both OTD1 and OTD2 neurons, there was a higher correlation between responses to similar molecular structure (Sk and XK,) than between responses to similar contingency (SK and ST) (OTD2: SK vs. ST R2=0.04, SK vs. XK R2=0.58; OTD1: SK vs. ST R2=0.13, SK vs. XK R2=0.40).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F-G

claim: 76.5% of VP neurons had a smaller absolute difference in the response magnitude to the 2 S odors than the absolute difference between the sucrose-paired ketone and the control ketone.
source: Moreover, most VP neurons (76.5%), had a smaller absolute difference in the response magnitude to the 2 S odors (|SK-ST|) than the absolute difference between the sucrose-paired ketone and the control ketone (|SK-XK|) (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 3H

claim: Only half of OTD2 and OTD1 neurons showed smaller |SK-ST| than |SK-XK|.
source: By comparison, only half of OTD2 and OTD1 neurons showed smaller |SK-ST| than |SK-XK|, as would be expected if response magnitude to an odor did not depend on reward-contingency.
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 3H

claim: The percentage of neurons that support intervalence classification increased regardless of region but this effect was markedly more pronounced among VP neurons than among OTD1 or OTD2 neurons.
source: Across multiple days of imaging, we found that the percentage of neurons that support intervalence classification increased regardless of region but that this effect was markedly more pronounced among VP neurons than among OTD1 or OTD2 neurons (Figure 3I–J, Appendix 1—tables 12–15, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, Appendix 1—tables 39–41).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 3I-J

claim: By day 6, there were thrice as many VP neurons with good intervalence decoding than with intravalence decoding.
source: By day 6, there were thrice as many VP neurons with good intervalence decoding than with intravalence decoding (51.8 ± 5.0% vs 14.4 ± 5.8% for {SK vs XK} and {SK vs ST}, respectively).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 3I-K

claim: A similar number of OT neurons displayed good intervalence decoding as did intravalence decoding.
source: In contrast, a similar number of OT neurons displayed good intervalence decoding as did intravalence decoding (20.8% vs 19.9% of OTD1; 12.8% and 21.0% of OTD2 for {SK vs XK} and {SK vs ST}, respectively).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 3I-K

claim: 46.9–57.8% of day 6 VP neurons had auROC >0.75 for any classification between a sucrose-cue and a control odor or airpuff-cue.
source: Whereas 10.2% of all day 6 VP neurons had auROC >0.75 for {SK vs. ST}, 46.9–57.8% had auROC >0.75 for any classification between a sucrose-cue and a control odor or airpuff-cue.
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H

claim: There were few VP neurons with auROC >0.75 for any classification between a puff-cue and a control odor.
source: By comparison, there were few neurons with auROC >0.75 for any classification between a puff-cue and a control odor (2.3–10.9%), suggesting that negative valence is either not encoded in these VP neurons or the negative valence was not learned.
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H

claim: Half of VP neurons were valence encoding by day 6.
source: According to this categorization, half of VP neurons were valence encoding by day 6, followed by OTD1 then OTD2 (Figure 3M and N; 47.7, 16.2, 7.3% for VP, OTD1, and OTD2, respectively).
evidence: Supported by categorization analysis shown in Figure 3M-N

claim: VP had a smaller percentage of identity encoding neurons than either OTD1 or OTD2.
source: The opposite was true for identity encoding. VP had a smaller percentage of identity encoding neurons than either OTD1 or OTD2 (14.8, 21.1, 22.9% for VP, OTD1, and OTD2, respectively).
evidence: Supported by categorization analysis shown in Figure 3M-N

claim: A majority of OTD2 and OTD1 neurons (69.7% and 62.6%, respectively) showed auROC <0.75 for both {SK vs. ST} or {SK vs. PK}.
source: However, the most striking observation was that while only a subset (37.5%) of VP neurons had auROC <0.75 for both {SK vs. XK} and {SK vs. XK}, a majority of OTD2 and OTD1 neurons (69.7% and 62.6%, respectively) showed auROC <0.75 for both {SK vs. ST} or {SK vs. PK}.
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 3M-N

claim: 17.9% and 20.9% of VP neurons were responsive to sucrose on day 1 and SK and ST on day 3, respectively.
source: When quantified, we found that 17.9, 20.9% of VP neurons were responsive to sucrose on day 1 and SK and ST on day 3, respectively (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal tracking analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: The odor responses to sucrose-cues were larger on day 3 than day 1 in 85% of tracked VP neurons.
source: Consistent with above observations, we also found that the odor responses to sucrose-cues were larger on day 3 than day 1 in 85% of tracked VP neurons, but only in 65% and 57% of OTD1 and OTD2 neurons, respectively (Figure 4H–I, Appendix 1—tables 18 and 19).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal tracking analysis shown in Figure 4H-I

claim: VP animals had lower PR (5.83 ± 0.80) than either OTD2 (9.61 ± 0.37) or OTD1 (9.24 ± 0.44) animals after training.
source: After observing a consistent decrease in PR with increasing n, we compared the PR of OT and VP animals by repeatedly subsampling a fixed number of neurons (k=15) and found that VP animals had lower PR (PRVP = 5.83 ± 0.80) than either OTD2 (PRD2=9.61 ± 0.37) or OTD1 (PRD1=9.24 ± 0.44) animals after training (Figure 5I, Appendix 1—tables 24 and 25).
evidence: Supported by dimensionality analysis shown in Figure 5I

claim: The first PC of each VP population was sufficient to train adequate {SK vs. PK} decoders (CV accuracyPC1=85.5 ± 2.7%).
source: Though the first PC of each VP population was sufficient to train adequate {SK vs. PK} decoders (CV accuracyPC1=85.5 ± 2.7%), all 15 PCs were required for comparable {SK vs. ST} decoding (CV accuracyPC1:15=75.1 ± 13.4%) (Figure 5J–L, Appendix 1—tables 26–29).
evidence: Supported by PCA-based classifier analysis shown in Figure 5J-L

claim: All 15 PCs were required for comparable {SK vs. ST} decoding in VP populations.
source: Though the first PC of each VP population was sufficient to train adequate {SK vs. PK} decoders (CV accuracyPC1=85.5 ± 2.7%), all 15 PCs were required for comparable {SK vs. ST} decoding (CV accuracyPC1:15=75.1 ± 13.4%) (Figure 5J–L, Appendix 1—tables 26–29).
evidence: Supported by PCA-based classifier analysis shown in Figure 5J-L

claim: In either OT populations, the first PC did not support good decoding of either {SK vs. PK} or {SK vs. ST}.
source: In either OT populations, the first PC did not support good decoding of either {SK vs. PK} or {SK vs. ST}.
evidence: Supported by PCA-based classifier analysis shown in Figure 5J-L

claim: Many VP neurons showed consistent increases in fluorescence time-locked to the onset of a licking-bout.
source: Indeed, many VP neurons showed consistent increases in fluorescence time-locked to the onset of a licking-bout (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: Across all VP neurons, there was a positive and significant correlation between a neuron's valence decoding ability and licking decoding ability.
source: Across all VP neurons, we observed a positive and significant correlation between a neuron's valence decoding ability and licking decoding ability (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D; slope = 0.41, p=2.2 × 10–10, R2=0.28).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: Mice consistently licked most during Lhi, followed by Llo and Nhi, then Nlo.
source: When quantified across animals on their days of highest lick differential, we found that mice consistently licked most during Lhi, followed by Llo and Nhi, then Nlo (Figure 6D, Appendix 1—tables 30 and 31).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from lick spout retraction paradigm shown in Figure 6D

claim: There was a lack of significant correlation between the single-neuron decodability of {Nhi vs NX} and {Lhi vs. Nhi}.
source: Furthermore, we saw a lack of significant correlation between the single-neuron decodability of two odors that had similar licking but different reward-contingency ({Nhi vs NX}) and the decodability of two odors that had different licking but same reward-contingency ({Lhi vs. Nhi}) (Figure 6I; slope=0.038, p=0.61, R2=0.0039).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6I

claim: There was a significant correlation between two pairwise comparisons that both had high difference in reward-contingency ({Nhi vs NX} and {Lhi vs LX}).
source: As a control, we saw a significant correlation between two pairwise comparisons that both had high difference in reward-contingency ({Nhi vs NX} and {Lhi vs LX}) (Figure 6J; slope = 0.60, p=3.8 × 10–10, R2=0.30).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6J

claim: Most neurons tended to have large ΔR2-valence or large ΔR2-licking values but not both.
source: We found that most neurons tended to have large ΔR2-valence or large ΔR2-licking values but not both, supporting the idea that two largely non-overlapping sets of VP neurons encode reward-contingency or vigor but not both.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6K

claim: Δlicking has a weak and not significant relationship with pairwise CV accuracy.
source: We found that Δlicking has a weak and not significant relationship with pairwise CV accuracy (Figure 6N; slope = 0.076, p=0.079, R2=0.042).
evidence: Supported by linear model analysis shown in Figure 6N

claim: Δreward-contingency had a larger and statistically significant correlation with pairwise accuracy.
source: By comparison Δreward-contingency (or P(S), as in probability of sucrose delivery following odor) had a larger and statistically significant correlation with pairwise accuracy (Figure 6O; slope = 0.15, p=3.7 × 10–4, R2=0.16).
evidence: Supported by linear model analysis shown in Figure 6O

claim: The combined model of Δlick and ΔP(S) showed larger coefficients and larger R2 than either single variable model.
source: The combined model, however, showed larger coefficients and larger R2 than either single variable model, suggesting an additive effect of both features on CV accuracy (Figure 6P; accuracy = 0.18Δlick +0.24ΔP(S) - 0.22Δlick*ΔP(S)+0.65, R2=0.23).
evidence: Supported by linear model analysis shown in Figure 6P

claim: Both reward-contingency and licking vigor are encoded in the population-level activity of VP neurons.
source: Thus, we conclude that both reward-contingency and licking vigor are encoded in the population-level activity of VP neurons.
evidence: Supported by analysis of lick spout retraction paradigm data shown in Figure 6

claim: The OT is composed primarily of Spiny Projection Neurons (SPN's) which express either the Drd1 or Drd2 DA receptors.
source: As with other striatal structures, the OT is composed primarily of Spiny Projection Neurons (SPN's) which express either the Drd1 or Drd2 DA receptors (abbreviated as OTD1 and OTD2, respectively; Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Coincident stimulation of the lateral olfactory tract and DAergic midbrain afferents supports LTP of excitatory current in the OT.
source: Coincident stimulation of the lateral olfactory tract and DAergic midbrain afferents supports LTP of excitatory current (Wieland et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: OT neurons are known to respond to a wide range of odorants.
source: And while the OT neurons are known to respond to a wide range of odorants (Wesson and Wilson, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: The most well-established target of the OT is the VP.
source: The most well-established target of the OT is the VP (Newman and Winans, 1980; Zahm and Heimer, 1987)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: VP plays a critical role in reward processing.
source: Although it is well-established that the VP plays a critical role in reward processing, there has been ongoing disagreement on what specific latent features are encoded by VP neurons.
evidence: Supported by general scientific knowledge and citations throughout the text

claim: Contrary to a previous report, both OTD1 and OTD2 neurons of the anteromedial OT project primarily to the ventrolateral portion of the VP and minimally elsewhere.
source: We began by refining our understanding of OT's efferents to reveal that, contrary to a previous report, both OTD1 and OTD2 neurons of the anteromedial OT project primarily to the ventrolateral portion of the VP and minimally elsewhere.
evidence: Supported by anterograde and retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1

claim: Reward responsive VP neurons gradually become reward-cue responsive.
source: By examining the same neurons across multiple days of pairing, we propose a putative cellular mechanism for reward-cue responsiveness in VP wherein reward responsive VP neurons gradually become reward-cue responsive.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal tracking data shown in Figure 4

claim: A high-dimensional encoding of stimulus identity is collapsed onto a low-dimensional encoding of motivational valence in the striatopallidal circuit.
source: These results provide a novel framework for the striatopallidal circuit in which a high-dimensional encoding of stimulus identity is collapsed onto a low-dimensional encoding of motivational valence.
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of OT and VP encoding shown in Figures 3 and 5

claim: Reward related signals are found globally throughout the brain.
source: These results, however, can often be difficult to interpret because reward related signals are found globally throughout the brain (Allen et al., 2019), and are likely multiplexed with signals about motor output and/or stimulus identity.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Dopamine serves as a neural substrate for reward-prediction-error.
source: One strategy has been to identify neural correlates of latent features assumed to be required for these algorithms (e.g. dopamine as a neural substrate for reward-prediction-error; Hollerman and Schultz, 1998; Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: AcbShD1 neurons project robustly to VP, LH, and VTA.
source: Consistent with past findings (Kupchik et al., 2015), we observed robust projections VP, LH, and VTA from AcbShD1 neurons and primarily VP projections AcbShD2 neurons (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: AcbShD2 neurons project primarily to VP.
source: Consistent with past findings (Kupchik et al., 2015), we observed robust projections VP, LH, and VTA from AcbShD1 neurons and primarily VP projections AcbShD2 neurons (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: Neither OT subpopulation from the anteromedial OT projects strongly outside the VP.
source: Contrary to one report (Zhang et al., 2017b) but consistent with another (Zhou et al., 2003), we observed minimal labeling in LH and VTA, or anywhere else in the brain, for both OTD1 and OTD2 experiments (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), suggesting that neither OT subpopulation from the anteromedial OT projects strongly outside the VP.
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B

claim: Strong labeling of soma by both CTB::488 and CTB::543 was found in the Acb, AI, and Pir.
source: We found strong labeling of soma by both CTB::488 and CTB::543 in the Acb, AI, and Pir (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1E-F

claim: Dense labeling of soma was found in various areas of the striatum such as AcbSh, AcbC, and CPu following CTB injection into the VTA.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Beier et al., 2015; Faget et al., 2016; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012), we found dense labeling of soma in various areas of the striatum such as AcbSh, AcbC, and CPu (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1H-I

claim: Some labeling of soma was found in some frontal cortical regions such as PrL, AI, and IL cortices following CTB injection into the VTA.
source: We also found some labeling of soma in some frontal cortical regions such as PrL, AI, and IL cortices.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1H-I

claim: The rare OT neurons that had CTB labeling from VTA were exclusively localized to the dorsal most portion of layer III, closely bordering the VP.
source: The rare OT neurons that did have CTB labeling were exclusively localized to the dorsal most portion of layer III, closely bordering the VP.
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1H-I

claim: In a valence-encoding population, odor pairs of different reward-contingency should be more different than odor pairs of same reward-contingency.
source: We reason that in a valence-encoding population, but not in an identity-encoding population, we should see that odor pairs of different reward-contingency (e.g. SK, a sucrose-paired ketone vs. PK, an airpuff-paired ketone) are more different than odor pairs of same reward-contingency (e.g. SK, a sucrose-paired ketone vs. ST, a sucrose-paired terpene).
evidence: Based on logical inference about properties of valence encoding

claim: Comparing neural activity in response to sucrose-cues or airpuff-cues can disambiguate between increased discriminability due to salience vs. valence.
source: Additionally, because both sucrose-pairing and airpuff-pairing should make the associated odor more salient, we can disambiguate between increased discriminability due to salience vs. valence by comparing neural activity in response to sucrose-cues or airpuff-cues.
evidence: Based on logical inference about experimental design

claim: Animals learn to associate S odors with reward in a flexible manner in the conditioning paradigm.
source: These results show that the animals learn to associate S odors with reward in a flexible manner in our paradigm.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing learning and reversal in Figure 2G-H

claim: Animals showed trends of behavioral changes in response to airpuff-cues, though they were not significant.
source: The animals also showed trends of behavioral changes in response to airpuff-cues, though they were not significant: during airpuff-cues, animals walked less and closed their eyes more than during other odors (Figures 2—4, Figure 5D-G, Appendix 1—tables 32–36).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D-G

claim: Animals show clear responses to the airpuff US indicating that they perceive the aversive stimulus.
source: However, animals show clear responses to the US indicating that they perceive the aversive stimulus.
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: OT and VP neurons showed heterogeneous responses to 6 odors across all 6 days of imaging.
source: OT and VP neurons showed heterogeneous responses to 6 odors across all 6 days of imaging (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by heatmaps of neural activity shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2-4

claim: Cluster I and cluster III most closely fit the description of putative valence-encoding neurons.
source: Cluster I and cluster III most closely fit our description of putative valence-encoding neurons, that is neurons that had similar responses to 2 sucrose-cues (SK vs. ST) but different responses to a sucrose-cue and a puff-cue or control odor (SK vs. PK or XK).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: Cluster I and cluster III were enriched for VP neurons.
source: Although all clusters included neurons from all subpopulations, cluster I and cluster III, which showed larger responses to odors predicting sucrose, were enriched for VP neurons (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by cluster composition analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Individual neurons in the VP were more likely to be valence encoding neurons than in either anteromedial OT subpopulation.
source: leading us to hypothesize that individual neurons in the VP were more likely to be valence encoding neurons than in either anteromedial OT subpopulation.
evidence: Based on inference from cluster analysis shown in Figure 3A-C

claim: Most individual anteromedial OT neurons have little discriminatory information about olfactory stimuli regardless of valence at the single-neuron level.
source: Thus, in comparison to the VP, most individual anteromedial OT neurons have little discriminatory information about olfactory stimuli regardless of valence at the single-neuron level and may be better suited in a population code.
evidence: Supported by single-neuron classifier analysis shown in Figure 3I-N

claim: Anteromedial OT neurons may be better suited for encoding in a population code.
source: Thus, in comparison to the VP, most individual anteromedial OT neurons have little discriminatory information about olfactory stimuli regardless of valence at the single-neuron level and may be better suited in a population code.
evidence: Based on inference from single-neuron and population-level analyses

claim: Sucrose pairing causes sucrose-responsive VP neurons to increase their responses to the sucrose-predictive odors.
source: Together, our data suggest that sucrose pairing causes sucrose-responsive VP neurons to increase their responses to the sucrose-predictive odors.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal tracking data shown in Figure 4

claim: In OTD2 odor-response, ||SK-XK||, ||SK-PK||, ||SK-ST||, and ||XK-XT|| were all similar.
source: When examining the average pairwise distance during the last second of odor, there was a relatively unstructured distribution of pairwise distance in OTD2 odor-response such that ||SK-XK||, ||SK-PK||, ||SK-ST||, and ||XK-XT|| were all similar (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by pairwise distance analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: In VP populations, intervalence pairwise comparisons were larger than intravalence pairwise comparisons.
source: By comparison, in VP populations, the distribution was structured such that intervalence pairwise comparisons between sucrose-paired and not sucrose-paired odors (e.g. ||SK-PK|| and ||SK-XK||) were larger than intravalence pairwise comparisons (e.g. ||SK-ST||, or ||XK-XT||).
evidence: Supported by pairwise distance analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: OTD1 populations showed an intermediate trend where most intravalence pairwise distances were smaller than intervalence pairwise distances with the exception of ||SK-ST||.
source: OTD1 populations showed an intermediate trend where most intravalence pairwise distances were smaller than intervalence pairwise distances with the exception of ||SK-ST||.
evidence: Supported by pairwise distance analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: VP population activity encodes valence but not identity, whereas OTD2 encodes identity but not valence in high-dimensional space.
source: Together, our population-level analysis indicates that VP encodes valence, but not identity, in low-dimensional space, OTD2 encodes identity but not valence in high-dimensional space, and OTD1, has some valence information and encodes identity in high-dimensional space.
evidence: Supported by population-level classifier and dimensionality analyses shown in Figure 5

claim: OTD1 has some valence information and encodes identity in high-dimensional space.
source: Together, our population-level analysis indicates that VP encodes valence, but not identity, in low-dimensional space, OTD2 encodes identity but not valence in high-dimensional space, and OTD1, has some valence information and encodes identity in high-dimensional space.
evidence: Supported by population-level classifier and dimensionality analyses shown in Figure 5

claim: VP population decoders were consistently generalizable when trained on odor pairs of unequal sucrose-contingency then tested on other odor pairs of unequal sucrose-contingency.
source: As expected, VP population decoders were consistently generalizable when trained on odor pairs of unequal sucrose-contingency then tested on other odor pairs of unequal sucrose-contingency (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by generalization analysis shown in Figure 5F-G

claim: OTD2 population decoders showed negligible generalizability across pairs of unequal sucrose-contingency.
source: OTD2 population decoders, on the other hand, showed negligible generalizability across pairs of unequal sucrose-contingency.
evidence: Supported by generalization analysis shown in Figure 5F-G

claim: OTD1 displayed a generalizability in between that of VP and OTD2.
source: Similarly to other metrics of valence encoding, we found that OTD1 displayed a generalizability in between that of VP and OTD1, suggesting that OTD1 could encode some valence in addition to identity.
evidence: Supported by generalization analysis shown in Figure 5F-G

claim: The VP population, on average, outperforms OTD1 at generalized valence decoding.
source: However, we note that the VP population, on average, outperforms OTD1 at generalized valence decoding (95.0 ± 2.0% vs 78.5±3.9%; Appendix 1—tables 22 and 23).
evidence: Supported by generalization analysis shown in Figure 5G

claim: Single-neuron intervalence decoding was worse in anteromedial OT than in VP.
source: After performing these population-level analyses, we noticed a discrepancy: although single-neuron intervalence decoding was worse in anteromedial OT than in VP (Figure 3M–N), population-level intervalence decoding was comparable between either OT subpopulations and the VP (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of single-neuron (Figure 3M-N) and population-level (Figure 5C-D) analyses

claim: Population-level intervalence decoding was comparable between either OT subpopulations and the VP.
source: After performing these population-level analyses, we noticed a discrepancy: although single-neuron intervalence decoding was worse in anteromedial OT than in VP (Figure 3M–N), population-level intervalence decoding was comparable between either OT subpopulations and the VP (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Supported by comparison of single-neuron (Figure 3M-N) and population-level (Figure 5C-D) analyses

claim: The encoding of odor information had a higher dimensionality in OT than in VP.
source: This led us to speculate that the encoding of odor information had a higher dimensionality in OT than in VP.
evidence: Based on inference from discrepancy between single-neuron and population-level decoding

claim: Reward-contingency and vigor information are both encoded in the VP but by different populations.
source: Furthermore, we saw a lack of significant correlation between the single-neuron decodability of two odors that had similar licking but different reward-contingency ({Nhi vs NX}) and the decodability of two odors that had different licking but same reward-contingency ({Lhi vs. Nhi}) (Figure 6I; slope=0.038, p=0.61, R2=0.0039). This decoupling suggests that reward-contingency and vigor information are both encoded in the VP but by different populations.
evidence: Supported by analysis of lick spout retraction paradigm data shown in Figure 6I

claim: Most neurons tended to have large ΔR2-valence or large ΔR2-licking values but not both, supporting the idea that two largely non-overlapping sets of VP neurons encode reward-contingency or vigor but not both.
source: We found that most neurons tended to have large ΔR2-valence or large ΔR2-licking values but not both, supporting the idea that two largely non-overlapping sets of VP neurons encode reward-contingency or vigor but not both.
evidence: Supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 6K

claim: The anteromedial OT to VP circuit is an ideal model system for examining how the encoding of reward cues is transformed across brain circuits.
source: Given this finding that VP may be the only robust output of the anteromedial OT, we proposed that the OT to VP circuit is an ideal model system for examining how the encoding of reward cues is transformed between connected brain areas.
evidence: Based on inference from anatomical findings

claim: The changes in anteromedial OTD1 activity are more likely to reflect increased contrast of identity or an intermediate encoding of valence that also encodes identity.
source: Specifically, information about sucrose-contingency in OTD1 resides in a high-dimensional space and generalizes poorly, whereas VP encodes reward-contingency robustly in a low-dimensional and generalizable manner. Thus, we suggest that the changes in anteromedial OTD1 activity are more likely to reflect increased contrast of identity or an intermediate encoding of valence that also encodes identity.
evidence: Based on inference from comparative analysis of OTD1 and VP encoding

claim: It is possible that other parts of the OT have extrapallidal outputs.
source: It is possible that other parts of the OT have extrapallidal outputs, as we only performed anterograde tracing from the anteromedial portion.
evidence: Speculation based on limitations of the experimental approach

claim: At least some of the VTA labeling Zhang and colleagues observed from anterograde viral tracing experiments could be due to backflow of the tracer virus in nuclei immediately dorsal to the OT.
source: It is also possible that at least some of the VTA labeling Zhang and colleagues observed from anterograde viral tracing experiments could be due to backflow of the tracer virus in nuclei immediately dorsal to the OT (e.g. AcbSh).
evidence: Speculation about potential technical artifact in previous study

claim: More posterior and/or lateral portions of the OT could have extrapallidal outputs posterior to the VTA.
source: More posterior and/or lateral portions of the OT could have extrapallidal outputs posterior to the VTA.
evidence: Speculation about potential anatomical connectivity not tested in this study

claim: It is possible that the neurons recorded in Martiros et al. are from layer III of the OT, whereas the majority of the neurons in the present study are recorded from layer II.
source: We note that the lens placements in our experiments are considerably more ventral than those reported in Martiros et al. It is possible that these neurons are recorded from layer III of the OT, whereas the majority of the neurons in the present study are recorded from layer II.
evidence: Speculation about potential explanation for discrepancies with previous study

claim: It is also possible that some of the neurons recorded in Martiros et al. could be from the rostral portion of the VP which lies immediately dorsal to layer III of the OT.
source: It is also possible that some of the neurons recorded in Martiros et al. could be from the rostral portion of the VP which lies immediately dorsal to layer III of the OT.
evidence: Speculation about potential explanation for discrepancies with previous study

claim: It is tempting to speculate that the encoding schemes would be similar between OT and NAc.
source: Given that OT and NAc share many anatomical, physiological, and molecular traits, it is tempting to speculate that the encoding schemes, too, would be similar between the two areas.
evidence: Speculation based on similarities between brain regions

claim: Bulk stimulation leads to activity patterns well outside the physiologically relevant range.
source: Given these peculiarities of the striatum, we predict that bulk stimulation leads to activity patterns well outside the physiologically relevant range and that this warrants conservative extrapolations regarding OT SPN's endogenous role.
evidence: Speculation about limitations of optogenetic stimulation experiments

claim: VP neurons display robust encoding of valence, in large part, due to the loss of odor identity information.
source: Consistently, it is likely that VP neurons display such robust encoding of valence, in large part, due to the loss of odor identity information.
evidence: Inference based on information theory principles

claim: OT populations may be able to encode information about the large olfactory identity space due to their high dimensionality.
source: By comparison, OT populations may be able to encode information about the large olfactory identity space due to their high dimensionality.
evidence: Inference based on dimensionality analysis

claim: The extensive inhibitory collaterals among SPN's play a role in enforcing the high dimensionality of OT activity.
source: We speculate that the extensive inhibitory collaterals among SPN's play a role in enforcing the high dimensionality of OT activity.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanism for high dimensionality

claim: It is possible that the conditioning paradigm was not sufficiently aversive for the animals.
source: First, it is possible that our conditioning paradigm was not sufficiently aversive for the animals.
evidence: Speculation about potential explanation for lack of negative valence encoding

claim: While negative valence neurons do exist in the VP, they were outside of the field-of-view.
source: Another possibility is that, while negative valence neurons do exist in the VP, as has been reported, they were outside of our field-of-view.
evidence: Speculation about potential explanation for lack of negative valence encoding

claim: The lack of evidence for OTD1 to midbrain connectivity challenges the dichotomy of direct vs. indirect pathways in the ventral basal ganglia.
source: Functionally, the lack of evidence for OTD1 to midbrain connectivity challenges the dichotomy of direct vs. indirect pathways in the ventral basal ganglia.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical findings

claim: The canonical model of basal ganglia connectivity inadequately explains the functional consequences of DA modulation in the OT.
source: Given the lack of clear differences in OTD1 and OTD2 projections, we think this canonical model of basal ganglia connectivity inadequately explains the functional consequences of DA modulation in the OT.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical findings

claim: It is possible that the excitatory VP activity during sucrose-cue presentation is driven mainly by the numerous excitatory afferents while the inhibitory VP activity is driven mainly by OTD1 and OTD2 afferents.
source: It is possible that the excitatory VP activity during sucrose-cue presentation is driven mainly by the numerous excitatory afferents (Pir, BLA, etc.) while the inhibitory VP activity is driven mainly by OTD1 and OTD2 afferents.
evidence: Speculation about potential mechanism for VP activity patterns

claim: Endogenous OT activity does not contribute significantly to explaining the bulk excitatory activity in VP.
source: In a third and perhaps the most parsimonious model, endogenous OT activity does not contribute significantly to explaining the bulk excitatory activity in VP.
evidence: Speculation about potential model for OT-VP circuit function

claim: It is unlikely that OT to VP drives large-scale shunting of action potential in the presence of excitatory drive from other areas.
source: Furthermore, given that GABAergic synapses from SPN's to VP neurons is likely dendritic (Bolam et al., 1986), we think it is unlikely that OT to VP drives large-scale shunting of action potential in the presence of excitatory drive from other areas known to respond preferentially to reward cues such as the BLA (Beyeler et al., 2018) or the OFC (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference based on anatomical and physiological considerations

claim: The mechanistic role of the OT in this circuit is to provide spatiotemporally precise inhibition to coordinate the integration of excitatory inputs onto VP.
source: We consequently propose an alternate framework in which the mechanistic role of the OT in this circuit is to provide spatiotemporally precise inhibition to coordinate the integration of excitatory inputs onto VP.
evidence: Speculation about potential functional role of OT in the circuit

claim: OT would function as a high-dimensional filter for VP neurons to adaptively scale its various excitatory afferents.
source: Under such a framework, OT would function as a high-dimensional filter for VP neurons to adaptively scale its various excitatory afferents.
evidence: Speculation about potential functional role of OT in the circuit

claim: OT to VP circuit provides a novel framework in which a high-dimensional encoding of stimulus identity is collapsed onto a low-dimensional encoding of motivational valence.
source: These results provide a novel framework for the striatopallidal circuit in which a high-dimensional encoding of stimulus identity is collapsed onto a low-dimensional encoding of motivational valence.
evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis of OT and VP encoding
